# Normal-form game catalogue {.unnumbered}

All reusable normal-form games are stored together in `_variables.yml`. A
lecture inserts a selected matrix with a Quarto variable shortcode, for example
`games.prisoners_dilemma.matrix`. The catalogue below renders those same
definitions.

## Matching pennies with an asymmetric stake

The zero-sum modification used in @sec-learning-br has the same sequential
best-response cycle as matching pennies. Its unique equilibrium assigns
probability $2/1003$ to $H$ for each player.

{{< var games.modified_matching_pennies.matrix >}}

## A zero-sum game with a pure equilibrium and a best-response cycle

The profile $(E,E)$ is a strict pure Nash equilibrium, but sequential best
responses starting at $(H,H)$ cycle among the four profiles using only
$H$ and $T$. Consequently, this game is not a potential game. See
@sec-learning-br-convergence for the argument.

{{< var games.zero_sum_best_response_cycle.matrix >}}

## Shapley's fictitious-play counterexample

This three-action game has a unique uniform Nash equilibrium, but
fictitious play initialized at $(a,e)$ need not converge to it
[@shapley1964, Section 5]. See @sec-learning-shapley for the update rule
and the first blocks of play.

{{< var games.shapley_fictitious_play.matrix >}}

## Hide the Treasure

Rows $h_1,h_2$ mean hiding in Box 1 or Box 2; columns $s_1,s_2$ mean
searching Box 1 or Box 2.
Entries give the Hider's payoffs; the Seeker receives their negatives.

{{< var games.hide_the_treasure.matrix >}}

## Morra

The row and column strategies $i\text{-}j$ mean raising $i$ fingers and
guessing that the opponent raises $j$. Entries are the row player's
payoffs; the column player's utilities are their negatives.

{{< var games.morra.matrix >}}

## A pure saddle point

Entries are the row player's payoffs; the column player minimizes them.
The saddle point is $(c,d)$ and the value is $7$.

{{< var games.pure_saddle_point.matrix >}}

## Two drivers choosing between two routes

Utilities are negative travel costs. Route $e_1$ costs $1$ with one driver
and $3$ with two; route $e_2$ costs $2$ with either load. See
@sec-learning-br-convergence for the convergence argument using a potential.

{{< var games.two_route_congestion.matrix >}}

## Cournot duopoly with seven quantity choices {#sec-game-cournot}

This is a finite instance of the linear Cournot model discussed in
[@monderer1996]. Alice and Bob operate competing firms. Each simultaneously
chooses an output quantity $q_i\in\{0,1,\ldots,6\}$. The market price is
$14-q_1-q_2$, and producing one unit costs $2$, so their profits are

$$
u_1(q_1,q_2)=q_1(12-q_1-q_2),\qquad
u_2(q_1,q_2)=q_2(12-q_1-q_2).
$$

The rows give Alice's quantities and the columns give Bob's:

{{< var games.cournot_duopoly.matrix >}}

An exact potential is

$$
P(q_1,q_2)=12(q_1+q_2)-q_1^2-q_2^2-q_1q_2.
$$

Every unilateral utility change equals the corresponding potential change.
Consequently, strict sequential best-response dynamics terminates by
@sec-learning-br-convergence. With Alice updating first and ties between new best
responses resolved toward the smaller quantity, the notebook's initial
profile $(0,0)$ produces

$$
(0,0)\to(6,0)\to(6,3)\to(4,3)\to(4,4).
$$

The potential increases through $0,36,45,47,48$. The pure equilibria are
$(3,5)$, $(4,4)$, and $(5,3)$, so changing the initial quantities can also
illustrate different terminal profiles.

## Inspection game

The inspection game of [@vonstengel2004, Figure 2], with rows and columns
reordered. The row player audits and the column player chooses whether
to cheat; see @sec-stackelberg-commitment.

{{< var games.inspection.matrix >}}
